cls: NSAID - propionic acid derivative (non-selective COX inhibitor)
pharm: Inhibits cyclo-oxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), reducing prostaglandin synthesis to produce anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic effects
quick: Oral 200-300 mg/day in 2-4 divided doses (max 300 mg/day; single dose <=100 mg)
Take with food or milk to reduce GI upset
Avoid from 20 weeks; contraindicated from 30 weeks (ductus closure)
Small amounts in milk; short courses generally considered acceptable
Avoid in significant impairment; use lowest dose, monitor
Use with caution; reduce dose, monitor LFTs
BP, renal function, GI symptoms, haemoglobin, LFTs on long use
summary: Flurbiprofen is a propionic-acid NSAID used orally for pain and inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis and other musculoskeletal and acute painful conditions; it is also available as an ophthalmic solution (to inhibit intra-operative miosis) and as a throat lozenge. The usual oral dose is 200-300 mg/day in divided doses (maximum 300 mg/day, with single doses not exceeding 100 mg). As an NSAID it carries the class BOXED WARNING for increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events (MI and stroke) and serious gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration and perforation. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration.
indications: Symptomatic treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis
Relief of mild-to-moderate pain and inflammation (e.g. musculoskeletal disorders, dysmenorrhoea, soft-tissue injury, dental pain)
Ophthalmic solution: inhibition of intra-operative miosis
Lozenge: symptomatic relief of acute sore throat

dosage.d: 200-300 mg daily in 2 to 4 divided doses
dosage.n: Maximum 300 mg/day; single dose should not exceed 100 mg

dosage.d: 50-100 mg as needed, up to the daily maximum
dosage.n: Use lowest effective dose for shortest duration

dosage.d: One drop approximately every 30 minutes, beginning 2 hours before surgery (4 drops total)
8.75 mg lozenge dissolved in the mouth every 3-6 hours as needed
dosage.n: Maximum 5 lozenges in 24 hours; short-term use only

admin: Take oral tablets with food, milk or a full glass of water to minimise gastrointestinal upset
Swallow tablets whole; do not lie down for about 10 minutes after a dose
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with treatment goals
Ophthalmic solution: instil drops as directed; avoid touching the dropper tip to the eye
Lozenge: allow to dissolve slowly in the mouth; do not chew
Do not combine with other systemic NSAIDs
moa: Flurbiprofen is a non-selective inhibitor of the cyclo-oxygenase enzymes COX-1 and COX-2, blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxane. Reduced prostaglandin synthesis accounts for its anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic actions. The same prostaglandin inhibition underlies its adverse effects on the gastric mucosa, renal perfusion and platelet function. Topically in the eye it inhibits the prostaglandin-mediated miosis that occurs during cataract surgery.

absolute: History of asthma, urticaria or allergic-type reaction after aspirin or other NSAIDs
Setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery
Active gastrointestinal bleeding or peptic ulceration
Third trimester of pregnancy (from about 30 weeks)
relative: History of peptic ulcer or GI bleeding
Hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular or peripheral arterial disease, heart failure
Renal or hepatic impairment, volume depletion
Concomitant anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids or SSRIs
monitor: Gastrointestinal symptoms and signs of bleeding

preg: Avoid NSAIDs from about 20 weeks of gestation (risk of fetal renal dysfunction and oligohydramnios). Use is contraindicated from approximately 30 weeks because NSAIDs can cause premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus. In early pregnancy use only if clearly necessary at the lowest dose for the shortest time.
lact: Flurbiprofen is excreted in breast milk in small amounts. Short-term use of the lowest effective dose is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding; prefer NSAIDs with established safety data and monitor the infant.
renal: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandins and can cause sodium/water retention, hypertension, and acute kidney injury, especially in volume-depleted or elderly patients or those on diuretics/ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in significant renal impairment; if used, give the lowest dose and monitor renal function and fluid status.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; reduce the dose and monitor liver enzymes. Discontinue if signs of liver injury or systemic manifestations (eosinophilia, rash) occur.

major: Anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin) and antiplatelets - markedly increased bleeding risk
Other NSAIDs / aspirin - additive GI and renal toxicity; avoid combination
moderate: ACE inhibitors / ARBs and diuretics - reduced antihypertensive effect and risk of renal impairment (triple-whammy)
Corticosteroids and SSRIs/SNRIs - increased GI bleeding risk
interactions.food: Take with food or milk to reduce gastrointestinal irritation
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive risk of gastrointestinal bleeding
interactions.diagnostics: May affect renal function tests, raise potassium, and prolong bleeding time; monitor INR with anticoagulants

common: Dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea or constipation
serious: Acute kidney injury, fluid retention, hyperkalaemia
Severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)
emergency: Haematemesis, melaena or signs of major GI bleed

monitoring: Blood pressure, especially early in treatment and in hypertensive patients
Renal function and fluid status (at-risk patients)
Gastrointestinal symptoms and haemoglobin on prolonged use
Cardiovascular status in patients with CV risk
counsel: Take with food or milk and do not lie down immediately afterwards
Stop and seek care for black/tarry stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, chest pain or stroke symptoms
Do not take other NSAIDs or aspirin at the same time, and avoid alcohol
Report swelling, rapid weight gain or breathlessness (fluid retention/heart failure)
Avoid in late pregnancy; tell your doctor if you are or may become pregnant
Use the lowest dose for the shortest time needed to control symptoms
pk: Analgesic effect generally within 1-2 hours of an oral dose
Plasma Tmax approximately 1.5-2 hours (delayed by food)
Analgesic effect roughly 6-8 hours per dose
Store at controlled room temperature, protect from light and moisture; ophthalmic solution as labelled
pearls: NSAID class BOXED WARNING - serious CV thrombotic events and GI bleeding/perforation
Contraindicated in the setting of CABG surgery and from ~30 weeks of pregnancy
Oral max is 300 mg/day with single doses not exceeding 100 mg
Beware the renal 'triple whammy' with ACE inhibitor/ARB plus diuretic
Avoid concomitant other NSAIDs/aspirin and alcohol; co-prescribe gastroprotection in high-risk patients
The FDA-approved US product is an ophthalmic solution for intra-operative miosis; oral and lozenge forms are widely used elsewhere
missed: For regular dosing, take a missed dose as soon as you remember unless the next dose is near, in which case skip it. Never double up. For as-needed pain dosing, simply take the next dose when needed within the daily limit.
overdose: Overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, drowsiness, headache, tinnitus and, in severe cases, GI bleeding, hypotension, respiratory depression, seizures and acute renal failure. Management is supportive with activated charcoal if recent, gastric protection and monitoring; there is no specific antidote and dialysis is not effective for the highly protein-bound drug.
